entities.summary:
Niccolò Fieschi (1456–1524), an Italian Cardinal from the powerful Fieschi family of Genoa, played a significant role in the tumultuous politics of the Renaissance Papacy and Italian city-states. His career, spanning from the late 15th to the early 16th century, placed him at the heart of curial affairs, diplomatic negotiations, and several papal conclaves, influencing the selection of at least three popes. As a prominent member of a family that vied for dominance in the Republic of Genoa and extended its influence across Europe, Fieschi embodied the fusion of ecclesiastical power with dynastic ambition characteristic of the era, deeply entwined with the political landscape of the Italian Wars.

Fieschi's ascent within the Church was rapid, benefiting from his noble lineage and legal training. He was created Cardinal-Deacon by Pope Alexander VI in September 1503, just weeks before the Pope's death, and subsequently participated in the October 1503 conclaves that elected Popes Pius III and Julius II. Under Julius II, a formidable temporal ruler, Fieschi served as Bishop of Fréjus from 1504 and later Administrator of the Archdiocese of Aix from 1507. His diplomatic acumen was further employed during the pontificate of Leo X, where he navigated the complex alliances between the Papacy, France, and the Holy Roman Empire, acting as a crucial intermediary in the shifting power dynamics of early 16th-century Europe. He was promoted to Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia and Dean of the College of Cardinals in 1521, positions that conferred immense prestige and authority within the Sacred College.
